Uniform Title: Janmamaraṇavicāra Author: Vāmadeva Editor: Śāstrī M. R.
Description: Photographed from volume 19 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.

Salutation to Amṛteśvara, whose body is that true consciousness. Now follows this [work],
a treatise on the investigation of birth and death.
*Bhūmikā* (Volume Number 19):
This work [is included] among the Śaiva Āgama texts.

This work was composed by the eminent Mahāmaheśvara teacher known as Śrī Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva, as a concise summary of the essence of the method for the knowledge of the non-duality of one's own self, which is the primary subject. And as for Śrī Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva...
He was a disciple of the venerable Yogarāja, who is also known by the synonym Śrīyogīśvara.
The venerable Yogarāja was himself a disciple of the venerable Kṣemarājācārya, who was a disciple of the venerable Abhinavaguptācārya.

At the conclusion of his commentary on the *Paramārthasāra*— a work on the specific essence of the Śaiva Āgamas composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta— the author indicated the name and other details of his own gurus; therefore, even though the time of the composition of this work is not explicitly stated therein, [it may be inferred].

Although Kṣemarāja was a contemporary of Śrīmad Abhinavaguptācārya’s disciple, this is so despite the fact that Abhinavagupta remained present in the world until the end of the forty-second century of the Kali Yuga.
By calculating approximately twenty years for each successive generation among his disciples, Yogarāja, and the authors of this work,
as well as during the time of King Ananta’s prosperous reign in Kashmir.

Based on the oral tradition of the people residing at the monastery of Vāmadevācārya, it is inferred that the probable time of the composition of this work falls within the final portion of the forty-second century.
Therefore, the time for the composition of this work is precisely that which follows it: the period of the final portion of the fourteenth century of the Kali Yuga.
Only a single original manuscript of this work has been observed; despite the greatest efforts, no other copy could be found anywhere.
This single manuscript, moreover, belongs to that version of the text described in the introduction to the *Tantrasāra*.
Among the collection of ancient Kashmiri manuscripts bearing Śāradā script obtained from the region of Āgarā,
this is one of the single-volume texts containing the *Uktatantrasāra*,
belonging to the library of the scholar named Kṛṣṇasvāmin.
It exists, having been written by the distinguished Kashmiri scholar [Viśeṣa] in the year 4603, corresponding to a nearby worldly year.

And yet, despite the brevity of this work, there exist within it [expositions] of those matters which have been determined in detail, as appropriate, in extensive Śaiva Āgama texts such as the *Śrī-Svacchandatantra* and the *Tantrāloka*.

Having gathered in one place the complete knowledge of all subjects— expounded in various places according to their utility as distinct methods for establishing the primary subject, which is the non-duality of one’s own Self— [this work is composed].
An exposition of the easily accessible and concise path, as follows:
(1) First, [the realization] of the self as the supreme Śiva.

Even though its nature is that of the entire universe manifested through its own freedom, there is the demonstration of its essential nature as Light, by virtue of its possession of unsurpassed powers such as absolute sovereignty which illuminate its transcendence over all.
(2) An instruction on the essential nature of the five powers belonging to Paramaśiva, known as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action;
(3) [an instruction] on that very Self of His, the luminous Paramaśiva, who desires to emit the universe.
The determination of the state of atomicity (*aṇutva*) is for the purpose of manifesting a contracted form.

And upon the attainment of that aforementioned state of atomicity, there is no loss whatsoever for the Blessed Lord—who consists of the vibration of unsurpassed bliss—due to being free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as space and time; on the contrary, [there is only gain].
This is the demonstration that nourishment (*puṣṭi*) belongs to the supreme majesty (*paramamahiman*).
3) (5) Of that very [majesty], which is connected to the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth (*dharā*).
The exposition of the attainment of the states consisting of the Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala [souls];
[and] of the atom’s sixfold sheath— consisting of Māyā, Kalā, Vidya, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati— which conceals its own true nature, as well as its karma.

The exposition: [This concerns] the four stages— nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, and śāntā— for one who is united with the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), which are comprised of the three objects of knowledge known as the worlds (bhuvana), the principles (tattva), and the arts (kalā), and the three means of knowledge known as the levels (pada), the mantras, and the phonemes (varṇa).
The description of the fivefold power (*kalā*) of the Supreme Lord known as Śāntyatītā, along with its presiding locus;
and thereafter, [the description] of the Blessed One who has resorted to the state of *āṇava*.
Manifesting the multitude of beings— whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or heat— through various types of birth,
lifespan, and enjoyments; and [manifesting] blood, flesh, fat, bone, and so forth, which exist in the state of *rasa* (nutrient essence) by virtue of the digestion of consumed food and drink.

Following the demonstration of resting within the seminal element (*śukradhātu*) by means of the middle self (*majjātman*), there occurs the manifestation in the form of male, female, and so forth; subsequently, there follows the enumeration of the major and minor limbs, joints, and their respective numbers, corresponding to the bodies of humans, animals, birds, reptiles, mosquitoes, and the like.

Following the determination of its accumulation, the state of remaining in the womb, birth, the subsequent stages of infancy and so forth, and the joy, sorrow, and other experiences undergone therein, there follows—
preceded by instruction regarding the attainment of future births, good and evil karma, and the resulting higher or lower worlds— [the teaching].
The illumination of the path of knowledge, which is the means for attaining the true nature of one's own self, has been presented here in summary.
Following the summary of this book, [it is established] through reasoned reflection.

I hope that discerning and learned scholars, through the practice of critical reflection, may attain the tasting of the essence of the fruit of knowledge of reality, and may they render fruitful my effort in editing and subsequently publishing this work.
Thus concludes the informant, Mānanīya Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍita Mukundarāma Śāstrī.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, whose body is nectar.
Now,
The Treatise on the Investigation of Birth and Death,
composed by the venerable teacher Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva Ācārya.
Having thoroughly restrained his inner mind, which was agitated on all sides by intense surges [of emotion], he generally maintains—

There is a certain, indescribable blossoming of consciousness within the heart that repeatedly overcomes the obstacles of the intense suffering of dissolution and manifestation— a root of bliss characterized by the delineation of ever-new aesthetic flavors. || 1 ||
Here, indeed, is the Self of the entire universe, both transcendent to all and yet consisting of all, whose nature is the light of consciousness uncontracted by conceptualization,
and who rests in uninterrupted bliss of consciousness.

There exists only the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose nature is consciousness, who is inlaid with all powers, and who alone manifests boldly at the limit of unsurpassed sovereignty; he is a great ocean carrying the flowing, dense, and manifold stream of the five breaths. His essential nature is light (*prakāśa*).

The power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) is autonomy; the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) is its wonder; the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the nature of self-reflection (*āmarśa*); the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is the capacity for union with all forms; and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is [the capacity for manifestation].
p.

2) Thus, although he is endowed with all powers, that Blessed One is metaphorically designated by means of these primary powers; and by the majesty of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), he makes his own self appear as if contracted.
Manifesting [itself], it is called "atomic" (*aṇu*). As it has been said:
"For Śiva is all-pervasive; yet, due to the seal of contraction fashioned by His own will, and under the influence of the flood of karma with its various fruits, He assumes this or that body."

Thus, the supreme gurus have understood this vibration of the power of Maheśa to be intent solely on the playful sport of concealing its own true nature; and so they have said: "Because it performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish, and because of its stainless sovereignty..."
The Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing His own nature.
Even though His own nature is unobstructed, that which constitutes the self-concealment of the All-pervasive Lord is indeed ignorance (avidyā),
from which arises this entire manifold world-process.

Thus it is said. And by this much, there is no impairment whatsoever of the Blessed One—who is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss and vibration, free from the limiting conditions of space, time, and form; on the contrary, it has been stated that there is a further nourishment of His supreme majesty.
If Maheśvara were to abide in a single, unchanging form, then his status as Maheśvara and his nature as pure consciousness would be lost, just like that of a jar or other such objects.
3) Limited luminosity is indeed the defining characteristic of the insentient;
consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so delimited.
Therefore, the powers of his own nature, surging forth from the great ocean of awakening, assume a manifold variety through their mutual collision, like waves.

And so forth. Thus, this Blessed One, by means of His own power of *māyā*— which is the majesty of His unfailing power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)— manifests Himself as if contracted by His very self, appearing as the *vijñānākala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala*.

It is thus accomplished. Among them, one who is joined with the single impurity of *āṇava* is called a *vijñānākala*; one who is joined with both the *āṇava* and *māyīya* [impurities] is the *apavedya-pralayākala*;
and one who is joined with all three—the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*—is the *saṃvedya* [pralayākala] by those very same [impurities].
The "sakala" (the conditioned soul) consists of the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dharaṇī*; for that very purpose, this creation of objects exists.
Therein, the Lord, intent on emission while abiding in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), agitates *māyā* by means of His powers and [produces] the *kalā*-principle.
From that [agency], it produces for the *pudgala* a certain degree of agency characterized by limited action;

from that, furthermore, it produces the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) called "limited awakening," and the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) consisting of limited desire. This is the principle of agency accompanied by attachment (*sarāga-kartṛtattva*).
That reality of time (kālatattva), though equal [in its nature], is divided into three ways—as past, future, and present—by which [the agent's] agency [is delimited] within attachment.

That which performs this delimitation is the principle of necessity (niyatitattva); this very group constitutes the six coverings (kañcuka-ṣaṭka), described as the external veil for the individual soul (pudgala) who is already enveloped by internal impurity (mala). Thus it is stated in the Cillācakreśvara-mata.
Māyā, kalā, śuddhavidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyatir—
the limited self possesses these six coverings (kañcukas) due to the power of obscuration.
And thus the internal impurity of the person (pudgala) remains like a cocoon; the cocoons are like husks, and therefore [the self] is devoid of knowledge and action.

Thus it is said. And that *kalā*, having manifested the limited agency of the *puruṣa*, creates the unmanifest (*avyaktatva*), which consists of the objects of experience in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion; from that, too, the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) arises, possessing eightfold qualities. From that, too—
The principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva) is divided into three groups according to the distinctions of sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic;

from the first of these egos, the mind (manas) is born, from the second, the sense organs (indriyāṇi), and from the third, the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi); from these [subtle elements] arise the gross elements (bhūtāni)—thus is this [manifestation] of the one and only Primordial God.

For one who wanders through transmigratory existence by virtue of the majesty of his own freedom, assuming the state of a limited subject, there is the expansion of the categories (tattvas). And it has been said:
"The elements, the group of subtle essences, and the senses are the root; the Person (puruṣa) is conjoined with the coverings (kañcuka), while the Pure One (suśuddha) is free from them."
From consciousness (vidyā) to power (śakti), this entire manifold expansion is the surging of waves from the ocean of one's own self-awareness.
p. 5) Likewise:
"O Sāla, O Uttara, O Puripuṇṇa, O Saalla, O Uttinna! Know yourselves!"
And he is equal to the most massive one.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that because of the diversity of the subjects (*pramātṛ*) regarding these aforementioned principles (*tattva*), there arises a diversity of objects of knowledge (*prameya*). To explain:

The earth-principle (dharātattva) is differentiated through the distinction between the possessor of power and the power itself; together with its own essential nature, it should be known as fifteenfold.

By this very same method, from the principle of the individual (puṃstattva) up to the principle of limited agency (kalā), the thirteenfold [category] is to be known as being like Rudra; such is the pralayākala.
In the same way, Māyā is to be known as ninefold; the Jñānakevalas are likewise [ninefold];
the Mantras are sevenfold, and the Mantranāyakas are fivefold.
The Lords of the Mantras, the Lords of the Lords of Mantras, and Śiva himself are not distinct;
moreover, he who knows all these principles (tattvas) according to their true nature [is liberated].
That guru, who reveals the potency of the mantra, is declared to be equal to me; those who have been seen, spoken to, or touched by him with a joyful heart [attain liberation].
"Men are liberated from sins, even those committed over seven lifetimes.
Thus, this sequence of principles (tattva-krama) has many conclusions. And as for the common form that pervades these principles in their respective groups:

(6) *ekarūpa*: that power (*kalā*) is so called because it is incapable of conceiving of a single form. Likewise, that from which the groups of principles (*tattva-varga*) recede is the power named *nivṛtti*.
And that [kalā] is established within the earth itself;
because it performs the functions of filling and nourishing while acting as the cause, it is called the kalā named *pratiṣṭhā*.
And it is established pervading everything from water up to the root.
Upon the dissolution of the object of knowledge, due to the predominance of pure consciousness, there arises the power called *vidyā*.
This power presides over the path beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*.
When the waves of the sheaths have subsided, it is called the power named *śāntā*.

And that [Kalā] resides from Śuddhavidyā up to the end of Śakti. This very group constitutes the fourfold egg (aṇḍa), characterized as the earthly, the primal-nature (prākṛta), the māyic, and the śākta.
Because it transcends all, Śāntyatītā resides within the Śiva-tattva.

Thus [it is said]. However, the supreme reality (tattva), because of its autonomy, transcends the *kalās*; one should understand that the worlds (*bhuvanas*) are likewise included within these very *kalās* as if they were *tattvas*. In this way, [the classification occurs] by way of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.

7) The object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been described as having a threefold form consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*), the principles (*tattva*), and the aspects (*kalā*); likewise, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also threefold, by way of the plane (*pada*), the mantra, and the phoneme (*varṇa*)—thus, [these belong] to one and the same [reality].

The repose of the perfect knower (*pūrṇapramātṛ*) as he transmigrates through the sixfold path due to his own freedom has been described. And here there are summary verses concerning the arrangement of initiation (*dīkṣā*):
One syllable of the *pada-mantra*, sixteen *puruṣas*, and "Dhareti" constitute Nivṛtti;
another is the *astra-mantra-pada* consisting of the syllables of the *tattvas*, three eyes, six, five, and four.
The fourth [syllable] consists of the syllable *muni*, the element (*tattva*), and the two-word mantra; the eighth vowel, the world (*bhuvana*), and the subsequent digit (*kalā*);
the syllable *agni*, the element, and the one-word mantra; and the first world. Thus is the fourth.
There are sixteen phonemes, one word-mantra, and one reality; this is the state beyond peace.

Thus, by resorting to this atomic mode of existence (*āṇavī vṛtti*), the Blessed One manifests the various classes of beings— namely those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, and from sweat— through diverse types of birth, lifespan, and experience. Therein, through the process of digestion of the food and drink that has been consumed...

For that which exists in the form of *rasa* (nutritive essence), there occurs a resting place within the constituent element of semen (*śukradhātu*), consisting of blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow; therein these living beings are born.
And so it is stated in the *Sauśruta*: "In this context, indeed, regarding food composed of the five elements, of four types, endowed with six tastes,
possessing two kinds of taste and potency, or eight kinds of taste and potency, and consumed in many ways..."

The subtle essence of that which has been transformed, which consists of the nature of fire (*tejas*), is called *rasa* (nutritive fluid). Its seat is the heart; and from the heart, having entered the twenty-four vessels—ten ascending, ten descending, four transverse, and [four] pervading the entire [body]—it [flows].

That aqueous rasa, by means of karma caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), daily satisfies, enlivens, sustains, and nourishes the body; having reached the liver, the spleen, and other organs, it acquires a reddish hue. Regarding this, there are indeed verses:
The waters within the bodies of embodied beings are colored by the vital heat (tejas) residing therein; when they are unimpaired and clear, those who know it call that "blood" (rakta).
From *rasa* alone, the female blood known as *rajas* flows forth;
by its power, it continues from after twelve years until the age of fifty, at which point it ceases.
The menstrual blood is fiery (āgneya), because the embryo partakes of the nature of both Agni and Soma.
From the nutrient essence (rasa) comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat is born; from fat, bone; from that, marrow;
and from marrow, the production of semen occurs.

In this manner, the nutrient essence (rasa) sequentially attains the state of semen through the flesh; likewise, for women, the production of the menstrual flow (ārtava) occurs in the same manner over the course of a month.

Thus, when such is the case— namely, when the blood and semen, which consist of fire and moon and arise from the connection between mother and father, [occur] immediately after the time of the flower (menstruation)—

In the mother’s womb, the semen becomes a *kalala*, then a *budbuda*, then a *peśī*, then a *ghana*, until there is the acquisition of limbs, the manifestation of limbs, the emergence of consciousness,
the perfection of all limbs, the circulation of vital energy (*ojas*), and finally the perception of pleasure and pain.
It is born. As stated in the venerable *Cillācakreśvara-mata*:
"From the mutual friction of the surging essences of the moon and the sun, when the fire has arisen and the central radiance has expanded..."
Due to the process of transformation into a pale-red state, the sprout comes into being; semen that has been emitted and has rested for one night reaches the stage of the *kalila*.
In seven nights it becomes a bubble, and in a month a peśī is formed; in the second month it becomes a ghana, and in the third month there is the assumption of heat.

In the fourth [week], there is consciousness in the limbs that were previously undeveloped; in the fifth, all the limbs are formed; in the sixth, the differentiation of all the limbs occurs; and in the seventh, movement arises.
In the eighth month, the vital heat (tejas) circulates; in the ninth, sensation occurs; and in the tenth month, the creature is born with a fully formed body.
Once born and touched by the wind, being crushed by the mechanism of the womb,
he does not remember the intense suffering produced through many previous births.
These causes of the body gradually undergo increase: the nutrient essence (rasa) effects its maintenance, and the blood thoroughly sustains life.
Flesh generally increases [the body], while fat clearly provides lubrication;
likewise, the bones maintain [the structure], with marrow as their inner essence.
Semen is said to produce excessive joy; urine creates moisture and separation;
and feces is proclaimed to cause the obstruction of wind and fire.

Sweat, moisture, and the necessary instruments, as well as the menstrual blood which is the cause of the embryo— having thus reached the body consisting of six sheaths through their appropriation [of these factors].
Disregarding his own true nature, a person looks toward external objects.

Thus [it is said]. And this very same meaning was also stated by the author of the *Nirukta*, beginning with: "One should know that the eight qualities mentioned belong to the earthly [element]; three are from the mother, three from the father," and so forth. In this very context, this definition of male, female, and neuter is given.
The cause of the three natures: through a predominance of *soma* there is birth as a male; through a predominance of *sūrya*, a female; through their equality, a eunuch (*klība*);
and through the differentiation of *vāta*, there is the state of having many offspring.
Thus it is said. There is also a distinction regarding its constituent parts:
"In the ninth or tenth month, by powerful winds of birth, the fetus is expelled like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish pain."
Its body is sixfold, and it possesses six layers of skin;
likewise, its bones are joined together in three hundred and sixty.
Including the large [teeth], there are sixty-four teeth and twenty nails;
the bones of the fingers and toes constitute four sets of four.
There are sixty bones in the fingers, two in the heels, and four in the ankles;
there are four bones in the forearms, and just as many in the shanks; two each are found in the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulder-blades, the sockets of the eyes, and the hips.
and one should point it out.
There is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back,
fifteen bones in the neck, one in the collarbone, and likewise one in the jaw.
At its base are two [bones], as well as those of the forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, and jaw; together with the ribs and their sockets, and the two arbudas, there are seventy-two.
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise the head;
the chest consists of fifteen bones—this is the collection of bones in a person.

Thus it is said. Among these very [locations], the designations are stated in other treatises according to the distinctions of *kapālabharaṇa*, *turuṇḍa*, *ruṇḍa*, *rucaka*, *nalayaṣṭīla*, and *nalakabheda*. He states the other locations:
The omentum, the kidneys, the navel, the pericardium, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine,
the colon, the bladder, and the rectum.
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus, and the two upper rectums—
this is declared to be the extent of the visceral cavity (koṣṭha).
The two pupils are the peaks of the eyes; the *śaṣkulī* are the earlobes; the cheeks are the temples;
the eyebrows are the two encirclers of the forehead; the lips are the *kukundaras*.
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the two masses of phlegm,
the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the tongue, the shanks, the thighs, and the two calf-muscles.
The palate, the interior of the abdomen, the top of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, the four eyelashes, and the feet, hands, and heart— these are [the locations].
The nape of the neck and other such locations within this body are the nine apertures,
which are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
"There are two hundred vessels and five hundred muscles.
According to Suśruta, there are thirty-eight vessels (dhamanīs) along with their branches located in the depressions of the breasts of women.
There are twenty-nine lakhs and nine hundred ligaments; furthermore, the continuous network of vessels and arteries should be known as fifty-six [thousand].
There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas), two hundred joints,
and fifty-four crores of body hairs.
Nine añjalis of rasa are to be known, ten of water, seven indeed of feces,
and eight of blood are proclaimed.
Phlegm is six [palas], bile is four, and urine is likewise;
muscle fat is three, marrow is two, and there is one and a half in the head.
The vital essence of phlegm is just so much, and the semen is just so much; this body is thus unstable—he who strives for liberation is truly one to be honored.
Thus it is for one who is healthy and possesses balanced humors (*dhātu*). Otherwise, however— due to the diversity of bodies, their lack of health, and likewise due to the humors (*doṣa*),
tissues (*dhātu*), and wastes (*mala*)— no fixed measure exists.
Thus it has been said. This very vision of the loathsome, which leads to dispassion, was sung by the sages in detail; and so they have said:
"A skeleton with pillars of bone, bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, and covered with skin—"
It is filled with a foul odor of urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of beings, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, subject to passion, and impermanent.
The Sage Pārāśarya also said: "Even for this physical body, which is a repository of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable..."
When it has been done, fools commit sins.
For one who is led toward death by means of food, how can there be delight through suffering? For who indeed would perform that which is devoid of dharma for the sake of the body?
Thus, having described the body, the nature of the embodied one is stated:
"Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon."
The self situated in the center of that maṇḍala is like an immovable lamp; it is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again.

This is the essential meaning here: having known that Self which is thus constituted, a person does not experience the affliction of rebirth; what is it like? It is that which exists within the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), numbering seventy-two thousand, as described in the Heart [Upaniṣad].

The lunar disc is situated within that [space], and those channels (nāḍīs) are beneficial through the accumulation of merit because they have the function of circulating the essence of what is eaten and drunk;
in the absence of that [merit], they are harmful. Their mover is one alone, though distinguished by different conventional designations.

The wind is fivefold, and among them two are primary—those connected to the south and north, consisting of fire and moon; through those two gates, the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs. (p.
Day is the downward movement of the apāna breath, and night is the upward movement; by this, the divisions of time—such as the half-month, month, season, year, and so forth—are also explained.
When the flow of the prāṇa is equal [in both directions], that is the equinox (viṣuvat); between those two, the third is the vertical staff-like state (daṇḍākārā).

The *brahmanāḍī* is situated there; the yogi, having restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*), perceives the Self in the form of a lamp. For this very reason it has been said: "One who is endowed with right vision is not bound by actions; [he is liberated] by vision."
But one who is bereft of it enters into saṃsāra.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, regarding the progression of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the sages have stated that its differentiation of objects arises from *kalā*; for instance:
"Coveting the property of others, and likewise thinking of undesirable things..."
And one who is attached to what is false is born in the lowest wombs.
A man who speaks untruth, a slanderer, and likewise one who indulges in idle chatter,
is born among beasts and birds.
One who is devoted to taking what is not given, who consorts with the wives of others, and who is a violent injurer of immobile beings by improper means, is reborn among them.

If it is asked, "Regarding this aforementioned application of torment, from where does this differentiation of the Self— which is of a non-dual nature— arise?", [the text] replies: "It is fashioned by the conceptual constructions of the great delusion of *māyā*," just as the single space appears divided within jars and other vessels.
Thus, although the Self is one, it appears as many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Thus [it is said]. And for one whose afflictions (*kaṣāya*) have not been ripened, the aforementioned form of self-knowledge never arises; and so it is said:
For just as a soiled mirror is incapable of reflecting forms,
so too an unrefined faculty is incapable of the knowledge of the self.

Thus it has been stated. Enough with further elaboration. In this way, that Blessed One, by the majesty of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), while assuming the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), being intent upon the acquisition of experience and possessing the full strength of body and vital breath, [acts] as described.

Awakened by the sequence of the sixfold path, he gradually assumes the acquisition of a body; as his past karmas are experienced, when the bodily machine begins to disintegrate through the six transformations of state such as old age and disease, there occurs stiffness of the body, trembling, and the contraction of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra).

In some cases, through inversion, its expansion occurs as the breaking of vital points (*marmabhaṅga*), emaciation (*śoṣa*), and so forth; thus everything that subverts the previous state is established until it perishes.
And although its destruction is momentary, nevertheless, it is described by way of a coarse mode of operation.
It is said to be manifested by groups of ten each; for instance:
childhood, growth, strength, wisdom, skin, sight, hearing, the sense organs, sitting, and lying down—these ten states of men proceed in groups of ten.
Thus it has been said. And so, when that bodily machine has disintegrated, that consciousness, assuming the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇana*), [proceeds] by means of the *ātivāhika* [body].

One body is led to another body; therefore, an *ātivāhika* (conveying) body exists in the interval between past and future bodies, serving as a vehicle upon which that person (*pudgala*) mounts and experiences the transition to another body. And it has been said:
In the *Kośabhāṣya*:
"That which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), so called because it has reached the destination to be attained."
Because it arises as a distinct occurrence due to its similarity to the continuity of rice,
the reflection is not established [as a valid example], owing to both its lack of proof and its dissimilarity to the illustration.
Furthermore, prior to death and subsequent to the moment of rebirth,
he possesses the discernment of his own class, pure karma, the faculties, and visible karma.
Thus says the Śruti:
"O Sūrya, O Brahmā, those who know the sacred law (ṛta) know your two wheels according to the seasons; but that one wheel which is hidden, only those who see the truth (addhātayas) truly know it."

The meaning of this is as follows: O Sūrya, O Blessed One, O Ātmaśakti, the knowers of Brahman (brahmāṇaḥ), those who discourse on Brahman, know your two wheels according to the seasons (ṛtuthā)—that is, at the proper times; "wheel" (cakra) is used here for the body because of its similarity to a wheel in its nature of revolving.

The duality of those two exists due to the distinction between the present and the future; therefore, by the reasoning stated regarding the interval between them, that which is one and called *ātivāhika* is "guhā"—meaning hidden and imperceptible.
For this very reason, they know it as "addhātayaḥ"; the intended meaning is that only yogins truly know it.

And likewise, in the waking state, at the time of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the sense organs such as hearing and the objects such as sound become the means of firming up for the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is in motion, the sense organs are active, and the desire to depart is the object;
concerning that very desire to depart, the preeminent sage Pārāśarya [Vyāsa] has established:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end, to that very state one goes."
O son of Kuntī, he is always permeated by that state of being.

Thus. This is the summary of the meaning here: there are three pre-embodied states of the body, namely, the experience of conception (*saṃbhava-bhoga*), the experience of birth (*janma-bhoga*), and the experience of maintenance (*sthiti-bhoga*). For instance, when consciousness has arisen within the womb, there is the experience of the embryo (*garbha-bhoga*).

At the time of birth, there is the experience of birth; for one who has been born, there is the manifold experience of persistence through the transformation of ages such as childhood and so forth; and there is the experience of death and the desire to depart—these two being the final states.
Among these, the experience of death consists of various bodily afflictions, while the desire to depart is [the state of] wishing to go forth.
Connected with the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) and directed toward that very state of desiring to depart, [the Lord] has declared:
"Whatever state one remembers at the time of death...
and so forth; for this very reason, [the scripture] speaks of benefits concerning past and future matters.
(18) "By [the word] 'remembering,' the application of the verbal cognition would be according to its true meaning; and this very point has been explained at length in the *Śrītantrāloka*."
This entire experience of death consists of the piercing of the vital points (marmans) and the impairment of the senses through delusion;
therein lies the total confusion of the organs and the state of being overwhelmed by labored breathing.
That which is this single final moment consisting of the vital breath is the fraction of time at the point of leaving the body, characterized by the separation from the breath.
In that state, whatever one remembers due to the awakening of prior latent impressions,
that very form one assumes, deluded by pleasure, pain, and confusion.
Thus [it is said]. And here, the classification according to the restriction of the objects [of experience] was made by the sage Vyāsa himself in the passage beginning with:
"But when dissolution occurs for the embodied one while *sattva* has increased," and so forth. These are the states of the body.
"In that five-spoked wheel as it revolves, all worlds are situated"—thus it is stated in such scriptural passages (*śruti*). Elsewhere also:
"Birth, existence, being, death, and the desire to depart—these are the five."
The transformations and misfortunes of the body.
Thus it has been said. In this manner, he is led from one body to another by means of that subtle, transportive body (*ātivāhika-deha*);
and that body, having attained awakening like one who has risen from sleep, continues to breathe.

By the wheel already described, that atom (aṇu) also perishes; revolving like the wheel of a water-drawing machine (araghaṭṭaghaṭīyantra), it transmigrates through various classes of bodies within saṃsāra.
And thus says the Śruti:
"Like grain, a mortal ripens; like grain, he is born again. Thus [it is said].
"Just as one casts off worn-out garments..."
This has also been stated by the sage Vyāsa in such passages as:

"Then, at some point, purified by the descent of the power of grace from the Supreme Lord through some means such as initiation, [one realizes] one's own non-dual nature, which rests in the bliss of consciousness."
Then he reflects upon and takes hold of his own essential nature, as stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of [his] fitness... and so on, beginning thus.

"Either at that very moment, or through enjoyment, upon the fall of the body one shall go to Śiva"—thus ends the passage. Alternatively, having spent the body in some temple of the Supreme Lord, one becomes the Supreme Goddess through the sequence of the previously mentioned rite; as it has been said:
In the Śrīsāttvatā:
"That place where the sound of a conch, issuing from the gateway of the temple, spreads in all directions is considered a Vaiṣṇava kṣetra."
That very same [merit] is proclaimed to be twofold when [the deity] is invoked by a sage;
it is remembered as being threefold when [the deity] has descended from a Siddha.
For those who have cultivated their selves, the fruit resulting from the self-manifested [teaching] at the end of the body is fourfold;
it should be understood that this occurs through the stages beginning with *sāyujya*.
The mind of men, which has been driven toward impurity by the power of the corrupt senses, attains complete purification at the time of death in the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus it is said. Also, in the venerable *Amṛteśaśikhā*:

"But those who have descended into the [lower] principles (*tattva*), who follow the command of Śaṅkara, and who dwell in the houses of self-born beings, sages, celestial seers, humans, and so forth..."
Having died, they reach that city and are initiated by the lords of the city in due order;
or else, descending again into the mortal world, they proceed to the supreme state by means of a boat.
Among them, the self-arisen ones (*svayambhuvaḥ*) are of two kinds: some are intent upon bestowing grace, while others have arrived for their own purpose and grant liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Thus it is said; even there, it has been stated that not everyone attains liberation:

"The state of being in the same world (*sālokya*) belongs to the mere initiate (*paśu*); the state of proximity (*sāmīpya*) belongs to one who has received initiation (*dīkṣita*); but for one who is intent upon that [liberation], the state of union (*sāyujya*) is attained—such is the command of the Supreme Lord."
But he who has gone beyond the higher scriptures and has abandoned all faith therein due to doubt—
he shall not go to the sanctuary at all, nor does he enjoy any fruit whatsoever.
But those who, with their minds, harbor hatred toward the knowledge of the seats of initiation (dīkṣāyatana), and yet practice that very [knowledge],
they all indeed go to hell.
And those whose consciousness consists of well-practiced [wisdom] and is indeed composed of Śiva are liberated while living; for them, there is no further deliberation whatsoever regarding death.
Thus it is said in the Śrīniśāṭana:
"Whether for the duration of milking a cow, the flight of an arrow, or the blink of an eye, one who is perfectly united with the supreme reality shall not undergo birth again."
Since he himself previously merged his own self into Brahman by means of another, how can there be any recollection for him when the end of life has arrived?

Thus it is said: "Even in the case of the venerable Śrī Rāma-bhaṭṭāraka, as long as the field (kṣetra) and the sacred ford (tīrtha) do not enter into Brahman, even a dog-cooker (śvapāka), having known that, is equal to me; there is no doubt in this."
Thus it is said: "Even by one who has lost his memory, whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, upon casting off the body,
he is liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge and, freed from sorrow, attains absolute isolation (kaivalya)."

Thus it is said; and in the venerable *Pauṣkara* it is also stated: "The knower of mantras, a devotee of the Lord, full of faith and always a believer, is established as the deity of the principles (tattvas) ending with the earth."

In whichever stage of life he may dwell, with his senses restrained and his body consecrated by the placement of mantras (nyāsa), he should constantly remember his own mantra residing within his own body.
"At the time of casting off the body, wherever one may find rest, having departed from one's own physical form, one indeed attains the primordial state.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well.
The body alone is the sanctuary; one should not go to any other sanctuary. One should resort to the single sacred mantra and avoid all other sacred sites.
p. 22) Thus:
"And those mortals who, O Nārada, remember me while their faculties are healthy and active..."
I remember them at the end of time as being like wood or stone.

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, one who is established as a supreme authority should not perform lamentations such as the shedding of tears, which are well-known in worldly conduct; as it is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāsana:
Weeping and corporal punishment are forbidden by all scriptures;
this is especially so in the Bhairava Tantra, where the Śambara rite is prescribed for those considered "beasts" (paśu).
"One should indeed abandon this improper conduct regarding the rites for the deceased.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Śrīmat Rahasyatilaka*, it is stated that for those qualified by the supreme method (*uttamanaya*) who maintain their own secret conduct, [this is prescribed] for the sake of preserving their reputation in the world.
The non-abandonment of those customs is likewise enjoined; for it is said:
"One must never cause the interruption of worldly custom—whether it be that which is secret, more secret, external, or internal."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding these two positions, the preeminent gurus alone are the authority for adopting either one. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śrīmahākula* that sacrifices, recitations, oblations, fasts, and so forth, dedicated to the father, must necessarily be performed after having propitiated the guru.

23) Even when the mandala has been merely outlined, with its sections partially erased, and is covered with dust as desired, one may enter it according to the prescribed rule even without having summoned the mantra.
Seventy million mantras make their presence felt there; how much more so the Kaulika tradition, which is invoked and worshipped therein?
O blessed lady, when dedicated to the ancestors, it then conduces to infinity.
Thus it is said; and in the *Śrīpracaṇḍabhairava* it is also stated:
"Those mortals who possess little wealth, though devoted to the Guru and the mantra, are especially incapable of performing the worship of the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyāga*)."
Then, for the sake of their ancestors, the wise man should worship that Siddhaliṅga;
there, the appropriate mode of worship is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
"In that [state], one uplifts ten generations of ancestors, both preceding and following.
Thus it is said. Also, in the venerable Bhāgeśamata:
"By means of poison, serpents, fire, epilepsy, hunger, overeating, and bondage..."
By outcasts, floods, thunderbolts, royal edicts, and thieves.
By great herds of cattle that had been scorched by the summer heat and drenched by the rains,
and by the utterly destructive methods of Brahmins, Mlecchas, and heretics;
Those who have been slain— those of evil deeds, those devoted to betraying friends,
others who have committed treachery against their masters, and likewise those who have brought harm upon themselves.
O lady of excellent complexion, for those who are pregnant, those of ill conduct, and those whose offspring have perished,
there is no other means of deliverance.
Without sacrifice, without fire-offering, without the formal assumption of a physical form,
and without the ritual application of the Great Net (mahājāla) for the extraction of the individual soul (pudgala);
"And the initiation known as the 'Resurrection of the Dead' (mṛtoddharaṇa), which pertains to all levels of the path" (p.
Thus, this is the procedure for those who follow the Higher Teaching (ūrdhvaśāsana). But for others, however—

The practice of what is prescribed by the tenets of one's own scripture alone is the highest good; therefore, enough of this. Thus, having ascertained the connection to the continuous chain of birth and death through the principle just explained, and having attained liberation while living (jīvanmukti) by means of the contemplation of one's own uncreated true nature, [one should proceed].
The virtuous take recourse in the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, as it has been said:
"Having understood the true nature of consciousness, they swallow the nectar arising from the extraction and pressing of the mountain-like heart-vigour from the ocean of awareness.
When this nectar is swallowed...
"Even regarding the *kālakūṭa* poison, if you gods were to drink it then, your state of being *Śiva* would be certain.
Thus [he spoke], having attained his established status through the grace of the venerable teacher Yogeśvara.
Vāmadeva composed this investigation into birth and death.
The women slow with fresh intoxication, the sweet compositions of song in the season of honey,
and the words with their graceful phrasing and secret meanings— alas, alas, they captivate the heart!
This treatise titled "An Investigation into Birth and Death" is hereby completed.
The work of the venerable and most excellent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva.

When the assembly of texts and learned scholars— the refuge of the six sciences— had undergone decline due to the passage of time, [this work was composed] for the sake of professional practice by one endowed with the vigor of true discernment, whose sole intent was the desire to uphold those various sublime Dharmas.

After deliberating with his chief ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious Sovereign of Kashmir established the primary office for the purpose of extracting the texts containing the essence of spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom. || 2 ||

May this book, having been refined through completion, purification, and exposition by virtuous men who have entered upon the livelihood [of service] under the supervision of Mukunda and Rāma, stand for the spiritual welfare of the good. (3)
The Tilaka.
May this [work] be offered to Śaṅkara, whose body is the immortal essence of the consciousness of one's own glorious self.
